bib.title: Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks

read.skipped: Trailing axis labels of supplementary Figures 11-12 only

question: How can we train deep neural networks that are robust to adversarial inputs, with a guarantee covering a well-defined class of attacks?
hypothesis: Training against a strong PGD first-order adversary on the min-max objective, with sufficient network capacity, yields robustness against all first-order attacks.
contributions: Study of the loss landscape of the saddle point problem: PGD local maxima are well concentrated, so first-order methods solve it, motivating PGD as universal first-order adversary
Network capacity matters: robust classification needs larger capacity than benign classification
MNIST and CIFAR10 models robust to a wide range of attacks, plus a public challenge

method.summary: Casts adversarial robustness as a min-max problem, attacks with multi-step l_inf PGD from a random start and trains on the resulting adversarial examples. Evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR10 with white-box, black-box and CW attacks.

datasets.name: CIFAR10
datasets.preprocessing: random crops and flips, per-image standardization

models.name: MNIST CNN
models.architecture: conv 32 filters, conv 64 filters (each 2x2 max-pool), FC 1024

other.capacity study: start conv 2, conv 4, FC 64, doubled up to scale 16

models.name: CIFAR10 ResNet (wide)
models.architecture: ResNet, 5 residual units, filters (16,160,320,640), 10x wider than original

training.objective: min_theta E[max_{delta in S} L(theta,x+delta,y)], cross-entropy on PGD adversarial examples
training.lr_schedule: CIFAR10 training step size decreased in steps (visible as drops in Fig 5)
training.steps: read from Fig 5: about 100k iterations MNIST, about 75k CIFAR10

other.train PGD MNIST: 40 steps, step 0.01, eps 0.3, random start, l_inf sign steps
other.restarts: no restarts during training; a new random start each epoch

inference.samples: Attacks: PGD with 1 or 20 restarts; single trained model per setting

parameters.MNIST attacks: PGD 40 or 100 steps, 1 or 20 restarts, eps 0.3
parameters.CIFAR10 attacks: PGD 7 or 20 steps, step 2, eps 8; CW 30 steps

metrics.name: adversarial accuracy
metrics.definition: accuracy on the evaluation set after attack

eval.protocol: White-box (A), black-box from independent copy (A'), from natural net (Anat), from architecture B (Tramer et al. 2017), CW loss attacks; eps sweeps incl. l2. No seeds or significance tests.

results.claim: Adversarially trained MNIST net keeps 89.3% accuracy under the strongest white-box attack (100-step PGD, 20 restarts).
results.setup: MNIST, eps=0.3 l_inf, 2 conv (32,64) + FC 1024, PGD-trained (40 steps, step 0.01); white-box source A
results.table: Table 1, row PGD 100 steps 20 restarts source A, column Accuracy

results.claim: Adversarially trained CIFAR10 wide ResNet reaches 45.8% under 20-step white-box PGD.
results.setup: CIFAR10, eps=8 l_inf, 10x wide ResNet, PGD-trained (7 steps of size 2); attack 20 steps
results.table: Table 2, row PGD 20 steps source A, column Accuracy

results.claim: Natural accuracy of the CIFAR10 PGD-trained wide model is 87.3%, below the 95.2% of the naturally trained wide network.
results.quote:
This network can achieve an accuracy of 95.2% when
trained with natural examples.

results.claim: A naturally trained MNIST net drops from 99.2% to 6.4% accuracy under FGSM.
results.quote: when evaluating on examples perturbed with FGSM the accuracy drops to 6.4%

results.claim: Black-box transfer attacks are far weaker than white-box: MNIST PGD from independent copy A' gives 96.0%, CIFAR10 PGD 7 steps from A' gives 64.2%.
results.setup: PGD-trained models, transfer from independently trained copy
results.table: Table 1, row PGD 40 1 A', column Accuracy; Table 2 row PGD 7 A' (64.2%)

results.claim: Local maxima found by PGD from random restarts have well-concentrated loss values (checked on 10^5 restarts), supporting PGD as a universal first-order adversary.
results.setup: MNIST and CIFAR10 standard and adversarially trained nets, PGD from random points in the l_inf ball
results.note: Text prints 10^5 as '105' due to extraction of superscript.
results.quote: we verified this concentration based on 105 restarts

results.claim: Robust training needs more capacity: small PGD-trained MNIST nets collapse to predicting a fixed class.
results.setup: MNIST conv net with 2,4 filters and FC 64, doubled up to scale 16; PGD training eps=0.3
results.quote:
attempting to train against a strong adversary (PGD) prevents the network from learning anything
meaningful.

results.claim: FGSM-trained networks overfit (label leaking) and give no robustness to PGD: CIFAR10 wide FGSM-trained model has 0.0% accuracy under 7- and 20-step PGD while 95.1% under FGSM.
results.setup: CIFAR10 wide, FGSM training, eps=8, white-box
results.table: Table 5, row Wide (FGSM training), columns PGD (7 steps), PGD (20 steps)

results.claim: PGD overestimates l2 robustness of the l_inf-trained MNIST model (gradient masking by threshold filters); a decision-based attack finds it much more brittle.
results.setup: MNIST l_inf-trained, l2 PGD up to eps=4.5, DBA 2000 steps
results.quote: PGD is in fact overestimating the ℓ2-robustness of this model

results.claim: First conv layer of robust MNIST model uses only 3 of 32 filters, each with a single nonzero weight, acting as thresholding filters ReLU(alpha x - beta).
results.setup: MNIST PGD-trained public and secret challenge models
results.quote:
the robust
models only utilize 3 out of the total 32 ﬁlters

results.claim: Min-max formulation: rho(theta)=E[max_{delta in S} L(theta,x+delta,y)]; inner max = attack, outer min = adversarial training; Danskin's theorem justifies SGD on gradients at inner maximizers.

limits: Only l_inf-bounded attacks are the focus; l2 PGD overestimates robustness (gradient masking)
CIFAR10 results far from satisfactory (45.8% under PGD 20)
Danskin's theorem assumptions do not hold exactly (ReLU, approximate maximizers)
PGD cannot rule out isolated higher maxima; robustness claim is empirical
Image classification only; no text or language model evaluation

terms.definition: attacks that rely only on gradients of the loss with respect to the input
